title: Parge coat and lime plaster for airtightness in old masonry
subtitle: Using a render coat on the internal face of solid walls to stop air infiltration without a membrane
excerpt: A parge coat is a thin render of lime or sand-cement plaster applied to the inner face of a solid masonry wall to block air leaking through mortar joints, cracks, and open-textured brickwork. It is the standard airtightness approach in pre-1919 buildings where a plastic membrane would trap moisture.
sourceNotes: AECB CarbonLite Retrofit Standard guidance on airtightness in solid-wall buildings; English Heritage guidance on energy efficiency in traditional buildings (2011); Historic England advice note on insulating older buildings; BRE BR 262 thermal insulation: avoiding risks.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin (3 to 6 mm) render coat applied to the inner face of a masonry wall to seal air paths through mortar joints and open-textured brick or stone, improving airtightness without introducing a plastic membrane.
An insulation material that allows moisture vapour to move through it rather than trapping moisture, suitable for solid masonry walls in older buildings.
Condensation that forms within a wall construction rather than on its surface, occurring when warm moist air meets a cold layer inside the wall assembly.

content.text: A
parge coat

is a 3 to 6 mm render applied to the inner face of an old solid wall. Lime mortar joints in Victorian brickwork, open-textured stone, and rubble-filled walls all allow air to seep through, even when the wall feels solid. The parge coat seals those paths without introducing a plastic vapour membrane that would trap moisture in a wall that needs to breathe.
In a pre-1919 house with solid brick or stone walls, a parge coat is typically the first step before applying
breathable insulation
. It costs a fraction of a full internal wall insulation job and can achieve a measurable improvement in airtightness on its own.
When a parge coat is the right tool
Solid brick or stone walls built with lime mortar (pre-1919 and many inter-war buildings). These have open joints and occasional voids behind the internal face.
Loft-floor-to-wall junctions: the parge coat bridges the gap between the top of the wall and the first rafter, closing one of the largest air-leakage paths in old terraces.
Behind timber-frame partitions in older houses where the air-leakage path runs behind the plaster and into the floor void.
Mix and application

The standard parge coat mix for a solid brick wall is 1 part NHL 3.5 (natural hydraulic lime) to 3 parts sharp sand. For a more airtight result, add a small amount of air-entraining admixture and apply in two passes: a 3 mm scratch coat, allowed to stiffen for 24 hours, followed by a 3 mm finish coat. The two-pass method closes pinholes that a single thick coat leaves.
Dampen the wall surface with water 20 minutes before applying the scratch coat. Dry masonry pulls moisture out of lime render too fast, causing shrinkage cracks.
Apply the scratch coat in a continuous sweep with a plastering trowel, working from the bottom of the wall upward. Use the trowel edge to rake a light scratch pattern before it stiffens.
Allow the scratch coat to stiffen (not fully dry) before the finish coat: typically 12 to 24 hours depending on temperature. Mist with water if the coat begins to dry out in warm weather.
Apply the finish coat by the same method. Feather into corners and around service penetrations.
Keep the finished coat damp and out of direct sunlight for 3 to 5 days. Lime carbonates slowly; rushing the cure causes surface chalking.
The condensation risk check
A parge coat alone does not change where the dew point falls within the wall. If the wall already had
interstitial condensation

issues, the parge coat will not fix them. If insulation is to be added behind the parge coat, model the dew point before proceeding. For solid lime-and-brick walls the answer is almost always to use a breathable insulation (wood fibre, sheep wool) rather than PIR.
What done well looks like

No cracks visible after a month. The coat feels firm and slightly flexible, not dusty or powdery. Air leakage through the treated wall section is reduced to near zero; a smoke pencil held against the surface in a pressurised test finds no movement.
What done badly looks like

A single thick coat applied to a dry wall that shrinks and maps-cracks within days. Lime applied in frost; the coat spalls off. A cement-sand render applied to an old lime wall that becomes the harder face and forces moisture through the masonry instead.

rows.symptom: Fine map cracking across the whole coat within a week
rows.cause: Coat too thick in single pass, or wall too dry at application
rows.fix: Hack off, dampen wall thoroughly, reapply in two thinner passes with a minimum 12-hour gap.

rows.symptom: Coat feels dusty and soft after curing
rows.cause: Mix too lean (too much sand) or cured too quickly in sun/wind
rows.fix: Scratch off the soft layer back to firm material. Mist the remaining coat and keep covered for 5 days.

rows.symptom: Coat debonding from wall in patches
rows.cause: Old paint, loose plaster, or a glazed brick surface not keyed before application
rows.fix: Hack all loose material back to masonry; apply a bonding slurry of neat NHL before the render coat.
